chunks.title: A habitat is the place
chunks.text: A habitat is the place where an animal lives and finds everything it needs. That means food, water, shelter from heat and cold, and somewhere safe to raise its young. A pond is a habitat, and so is a forest, a field, a rock crevice, and even the space under the roof tiles of a house. Animals are not scattered about at random. Each kind lives where its body and its habits suit the surroundings, and moving it somewhere quite different usually means it cannot find food or hide from whatever hunts it.

chunks.title: India has habitats of very
chunks.text: India has habitats of very many kinds, and very different animals living in each of them. The Thar desert in the west is hot and dry, and camels, chinkara and desert foxes live there. The Sundarbans on the eastern coast is a tangle of salty mangrove swamp, and tigers there swim between the islands. The high Himalaya is cold and thin aired, home to the yak and the snow leopard. The rainy forests of the Western Ghats are thick with frogs, hornbills and elephants, and the dry Gir forest in Gujarat holds the only wild lions left in Asia.

The Sundarbans on the eastern coast is a tangle of salty mangrove swamp, and tigers there swim between the islands.

chunks.title: Adaptation means the special features
chunks.text: Adaptation means the special features and habits that fit an animal to the place it lives. These are not choices the animal makes. They are built into its body, and they developed slowly over an enormous number of generations, because the individuals that happened to be better suited survived to have more young. Thick fur suits a cold mountain, wide flat feet suit soft sand, and a long sticky tongue suits an animal that eats ants. The same body that works beautifully in one habitat can be quite useless in another.

They are built into its body, and they developed slowly over an enormous number of generations, because the individuals that happened to be better suited survived to have more young.

chunks.title: The camel is built for
chunks.text: The camel is built for the desert, and its hump stores fat, not water, which surprises most people. That fat is a food store it can live off when there is nothing to eat, and keeping it in one lump on the back rather than spread under the skin helps the rest of the body lose heat. Long legs hold the camel well above the burning sand. Broad padded feet stop it sinking in. It can close its nostrils against blowing sand, and its long thick eyelashes keep the grit out of its eyes.

chunks.title: Fish are shaped and equipped
chunks.text: Fish are shaped and equipped for a life in water. A fish does not breathe water. It takes in the oxygen that is dissolved in the water, using gills, which are feathery organs behind the head. Water comes in at the mouth, passes over the gills where oxygen crosses into the blood, and flows out at the sides. A smooth pointed body slips through water with little resistance, fins keep the fish steady and help it turn, and the tail pushes it forward. Overlapping scales protect the skin and let it slide along easily.

chunks.title: Birds are built to be
chunks.text: Birds are built to be light enough to fly. Their bones are hollow with thin struts inside, which keeps them strong without being heavy. Feathers weigh very little and give a wide surface to push against the air, and the wings are worked by big chest muscles anchored to a deep breastbone. Birds have no teeth, which would be heavy, and they grind their food inside instead. Not every bird flies. The ostrich and the emu run instead, and penguins use their wings to swim, so wings are not only for the air.

Feathers weigh very little and give a wide surface to push against the air, and the wings are worked by big chest muscles anchored to a deep breastbone.

chunks.title: Beaks are tools, and each
chunks.text: Beaks are tools, and each one is shaped by what that bird eats. A parrot has a short thick curved beak for cracking hard seeds and fruit stones. A sparrow has a small strong cone shaped beak for picking up grain. A heron has a long pointed beak for spearing fish in shallow water, and a duck has a broad flat one for sifting food out of mud. An eagle has a sharp hooked beak for tearing meat. Look at a bird's beak and you can usually make a good guess at its meal, without ever seeing it eat.

chunks.title: Frogs live one life in
chunks.text: Frogs live one life in water and another on land. A frog lays its eggs in water, and out of them come tadpoles, which have a tail, no legs, and gills for taking oxygen out of the water like a fish. As a tadpole grows, legs appear, the tail shrinks away, and lungs develop in place of the gills. The adult frog can then hop about on land, though it must return to water to breed. A frog also takes in some oxygen through its skin, so that skin has to stay damp.

chunks.title: Snakes and lizards are reptiles,
chunks.text: Snakes and lizards are reptiles, and their skin is dry and smooth, not slimy. That mistake comes from confusing them with frogs. Reptiles have scaly skin that holds water in, which is why so many of them manage in dry places. They cannot make their own body heat, so they lie in the morning sun to warm up and move into shade when they are too hot. Most kinds of snake in India are not venomous, but you can never tell by looking, so the rule is simple. Never touch a snake, and never corner one.

chunks.title: Insects are the largest group
chunks.text: Insects are the largest group of animals on earth, and they follow one clear plan. An insect has six legs and a body in three parts, a head, a middle part where the legs attach, and an abdomen behind. Most have wings as adults. Ants, bees, beetles, grasshoppers, butterflies and mosquitoes are all insects. A spider is not an insect, because it has eight legs and a body in two parts, and a centipede is not one either. Counting the legs is the quickest way to settle the question.

chunks.title: Animals are grouped by what
chunks.text: Animals are grouped by what they eat. Herbivores eat only plants, and cows, goats, deer, elephants and rabbits are all herbivores. Carnivores eat other animals, and the tiger, the eagle and the frog are carnivores. Omnivores eat both, and crows, bears, pigs and human beings fall into this group. Teeth give the answer away. A plant eater has broad flat teeth for grinding tough leaves and grass, while a meat eater has long pointed teeth for gripping and tearing, and its jaws work like scissors rather than like a grindstone.
chunks.explain: Animals are grouped by what they eat. Herbivores eat only plants, and cows, goats, deer, elephants and rabbits are all herbivores. Carnivores eat other animals, and the tiger, the eagle and the frog are carnivores.

chunks.title: A food chain shows who
chunks.text: A food chain shows who eats whom, and every one of them begins with the sun. Green plants catch sunlight and make their own food, so they come first and are called producers. Grass is eaten by a grasshopper, the grasshopper is eaten by a frog, the frog is eaten by a snake, and the snake is eaten by an eagle. At each step some of the energy is used up in simply staying alive, so the chain cannot go on for ever. That is why there are always far more grasshoppers in a field than there are eagles above it.

Grass is eaten by a grasshopper, the grasshopper is eaten by a frog, the frog is eaten by a snake, and the snake is eaten by an eagle.

chunks.title: A food web is what
chunks.text: A food web is what you get when you notice that most animals eat more than one thing. A frog eats many kinds of insect, and many different animals eat frogs, so the neat chains cross over one another into a web. This is why removing one animal has effects nobody expects. When snakes are killed off around a village, the rats they used to eat multiply, and the rats go straight into the grain store. Every creature in a web is holding something else in check, including the ones people dislike.

chunks.title: Decomposers are the animals and
chunks.text: Decomposers are the animals and tiny living things that clean up the dead. Fungi, bacteria, earthworms, termites and beetle grubs feed on fallen leaves, dead wood and dead animals, and they break all of it down into simple substances that soak back into the soil. Plants then take those substances up through their roots and grow. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up year after year and the nutrients locked inside it would never return. Rotting looks like waste and mess, but it is really the world putting things back into circulation.

chunks.title: Many birds migrate, which means
chunks.text: Many birds migrate, which means travelling long distances every year and returning. They do it to follow food and to escape harsh weather, not because they lose their way. Bar headed geese fly over the Himalaya to spend the winter on Indian lakes and wetlands, and flamingos gather in great pink crowds on the coasts of Gujarat and near Mumbai. Places like Chilika lake in Odisha fill up with visiting birds every winter and empty again in spring. The birds find their way using the sun, the stars and the earth's magnetism.

chunks.title: Camouflage is colouring or shape
chunks.text: Camouflage is colouring or shape that lets an animal blend into its surroundings. A stick insect looks so like a dry twig that a bird passes over it. A grasshopper is green among green leaves and brown in dry grass. A tiger's stripes look bold in a zoo but break up its outline completely in tall sunlit grass, which is exactly the point. Camouflage protects the hunted, and it also helps the hunter get close. A chameleon can change its colour, which helps it hide and also signals its mood to other chameleons.

chunks.title: Animals build homes for shelter
chunks.text: Animals build homes for shelter and for raising their young. A weaver bird knots strips of grass into a hanging nest with the entrance underneath, so that snakes and squirrels struggle to get in. Rabbits and rats dig burrows, honeybees build wax combs, spiders spin webs that are both home and trap, and termites raise hard mud mounds that stay cool inside while the ground outside bakes. Most animals do not live in their homes all the time. A nest is usually built for the eggs and abandoned once the young can fly.

chunks.title: Mammals are the animals that
chunks.text: Mammals are the animals that have hair on their bodies and feed their young on milk. Cows, goats, dogs, monkeys, elephants, bats and humans are all mammals. A whale is a mammal too, and not a fish, however much it looks like one. A whale has no gills. It must come up to the surface to breathe air through a hole on top of its head, and it feeds its calf on milk. Bats are mammals that truly fly, and the fruit bats you see hanging in big trees at dusk are the largest bats in India.

chunks.title: Bats and owls hunt in
chunks.text: Bats and owls hunt in the dark, and they have unusual ways of finding their way. Many bats send out squeaks far too high for us to hear, listen for the echo bouncing back, and work out from it where a wall or a moth is. This is why a bat can fly through a black cave without touching anything. Owls have enormous eyes that gather what little light there is, and their feathers are edged softly so that they fly almost silently. Night hunters are usually eating the insects and rats that come out after dark.

chunks.title: Animals are in trouble mainly
chunks.text: Animals are in trouble mainly because their habitats are disappearing. When a forest is cleared, a wetland is drained or a grassland is built over, the animals living there lose their food and their shelter all at once, and most cannot simply move elsewhere because that land is already taken. Hunting and pollution add to it. India protects animals through national parks and sanctuaries, and Project Tiger, begun in nineteen seventy three, set aside reserves where tigers could breed safely. Protecting a habitat protects every creature in it at the same time.

Hunting and pollution add to it.

chunks.title: Wild animals should be watched
chunks.text: Wild animals should be watched and not touched, and this is for their sake as much as yours. A wild animal that is fed by people stops looking for its own food and starts coming into villages, which usually ends badly for the animal. Handling a young bird or a fawn can make its parents abandon it. Monkeys that are fed become bold and snatch. The right way to enjoy wild animals is to stay still and quiet at a distance and watch what they do, which is far more interesting than anything that happens when they run away.
